Introduction

The Internet of Things (IoT) has changed the organization of modern healthcare by connecting wearable sensors, implantable devices, bedside monitors, and clinical information systems. Within the Internet of Health Things (IoHT), these devices continuously collect and exchange physiological and operational data to support remote monitoring, early intervention, and more efficient use of hospital resources [1–6]. This connectivity is valuable, but it also creates heterogeneous, high-dimensional traffic streams whose statistical properties vary across devices, protocols, and clinical settings. Accurate analysis of such traffic must therefore account for nonlinear relationships, temporal dependencies, noisy attributes, and uneven class distributions [7,8].

Security is especially important because malicious traffic in an IoHT environment can affect both information confidentiality and patient safety. Distributed denial-of-service attacks, spoofing, data injection, and man-in-the-middle activity may interrupt clinical communication or alter telemetry used in time-sensitive decisions [9–12]. An effective intrusion detection system must identify these events with high sensitivity while limiting false alarms, since excessive alerts can burden clinical and technical staff and reduce confidence in automated monitoring tools [13].

Traditional classifiers, including logistic regression, decision trees, and support vector machines, remain useful because of their modest computational requirements [14–16]. However, their performance may decline when attack patterns are distributed across many correlated features or develop over time. Deep models such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, and generative architectures can learn richer representations [17–19], but they may require careful hyperparameter selection and substantial computational resources. These constraints are important in IoHT gateways and edge devices, where memory, energy, and response time are limited [20].

Hybrid architectures offer a practical way to balance representation quality and computational cost. A one-dimensional CNN can extract short-range relationships among traffic attributes, whereas LSTM and Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) layers capture longer and rapidly changing sequential patterns. Multi-head attention further allows the model to assign greater weight to the positions that are most informative for distinguishing benign and malicious traffic [21–25]. Nevertheless, existing studies often evaluate only one dataset, depend on manually selected parameters, or report high accuracy without examining feature reduction, convergence behavior, and cross-dataset consistency.

To address these limitations, this study proposes a Lionfish-optimized CNN-LSTM-GRU-Attention framework for binary IoHT intrusion detection. The pipeline first removes redundant records and non-informative fields, applies analysis of variance (ANOVA) feature selection, and standardizes the retained variables. Lionfish Optimization then searches for an effective combination of learning rate, convolutional depth, filter number, LSTM units, and GRU units. The selected configuration is trained and evaluated on three heterogeneous benchmarks: ECU-IoHT, WUSTL-EHMS-2020, and DSICU. The main contributions of this study are as follows:

A unified CNN-LSTM-GRU-Attention architecture is developed to learn local feature interactions, long-term dependencies, rapid temporal changes, and context-sensitive attack indicators within one trainable model.
A Lionfish Optimization procedure is integrated to select key architectural and learning parameters systematically, reducing dependence on manual trial-and-error tuning.

A consistent preprocessing pipeline combines duplicate removal, leakage-aware partitioning, ANOVA-based feature selection, and z-score standardization to improve data quality and reduce irrelevant variation.

The framework is evaluated across three distinct healthcare and telemetry datasets, and its performance is examined through accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, confusion matrices, convergence behavior, training time, and comparison with recent methods.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related intrusion-detection studies and identifies the unresolved gaps. Section 3 presents the datasets, preprocessing stages, Lionfish Optimization procedure, and hybrid network architecture. Section 4 reports the experimental findings, comparative analysis, discussion, and study limitations. Section 5 concludes the paper and outlines directions for further research.

Table 1: Related Works

The studies summarized in Table 1 confirm that high classification accuracy is achievable in IoHT intrusion detection, but several limitations remain. Many approaches are validated on a single benchmark, rely on centralized or static training conditions, and provide limited evidence of robustness when the traffic distribution changes. Other methods use complex ensembles, quantum-inspired components, or manually configured fuzzy rules that increase computational cost and reduce suitability for resource-constrained healthcare gateways. In addition, several studies focus mainly on overall accuracy, while giving less attention to minority attack classes, false-negative behavior, convergence stability, and the effect of feature redundancy.

The proposed framework addresses these gaps through a compact and integrated design. ANOVA-based feature selection removes weak predictors before training, while z-score standardization reduces scale-related bias. The CNN component captures local interactions, the LSTM and GRU layers model complementary temporal dependencies, and multi-head attention emphasizes the most informative positions. Lionfish Optimization replaces manual parameter selection with a data-driven search process. Finally, evaluation on ECU-IoHT, WUSTL-EHMS-2020, and DSICU provides broader evidence of cross-dataset consistency than studies restricted to one traffic source.
